explanations.answer: Go and do all that is in your heart
explanations.explanation: Nathan, the prophet, tells the king, "Go and do all that is in your heart…" (2 Samuel 7:3). That's a big yes for David's idea. I know that feeling, friend. Somebody asks if you want another cookie and you answer before they finish asking.

explanations.answer: Wait until the LORD speaks to you
explanations.explanation: Nathan doesn't tell David to wait. He says, "Go and do all that is in your heart…" (2 Samuel 7:3). The LORD does speak, but it's that night, and it comes to Nathan (2 Samuel 7:4). So Nathan says go first, and the waiting is nowhere in his words.

explanations.answer: Leave the ark right where it is
explanations.explanation: Nathan says nothing about leaving the ark in its tent. His words to David are, "Go and do all that is in your heart…" (2 Samuel 7:3). That's a green light, not a red one. Nobody gets told to sit tight in this verse.

Nathan finishes his answer with "…for the LORD is with you." (2 Samuel 7:3). That's the reason he gives, and it's a true thing to say about David. Nathan says it with a lot of confidence. I'd have said it too, and then I'd have checked the oven twice.

Nathan never mentions the people in his answer. The reason he gives is "…for the LORD is with you." (2 Samuel 7:3). The text puts the LORD in the reason and leaves a crowd out of it. Applause isn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: The ark has waited long enough
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, since David was the one bothered by the ark in a tent. But Nathan doesn't say it. He says, "…for the LORD is with you." (2 Samuel 7:3). The ark's waiting time never comes up in his answer.

The LORD opens with a question: "Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in?" (2 Samuel 7:5). He starts with a question, not a list of orders. David came in with a plan and got a question back. I know that feeling from my own plans for a second batch.

It really does start with a question. The LORD says, "Are you the one to build for Me a house to dwell in?" (2 Samuel 7:5). David had just made a statement about cedar and a tent. Now he gets asked something instead.

The text says the opposite. God asks, "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people Israel, 'Why haven't you built Me a house of cedar?'" (2 Samuel 7:7). The way He puts the question, nobody ever got asked. He never nagged anybody about cedar.

That's right. God asks whether He ever said to any leader, "Why haven't you built Me a house of cedar?" (2 Samuel 7:7). The question points to a no. He wasn't dropping hints. I've dropped hints about my apron needing a wash, so I know the type, and this isn't it.

explanations.answer: In the pasture following the flock
explanations.explanation: God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." (2 Samuel 7:8). David went from walking behind sheep to ruling a nation. That's a career jump you don't see on a resume every day. God starts his message to David right there, at the beginning.

explanations.answer: At the threshing floor of Nacon
explanations.explanation: The threshing floor of Nacon is a spot from the ark's journey (2 Samuel 6:6), not from David's start. In this passage God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock…" (2 Samuel 7:8). David's story begins with the flock, and that's where God starts.

explanations.answer: In the house of Abinadab on the hill
explanations.explanation: Abinadab's house on the hill is where the ark had been (2 Samuel 6:3). It isn't where God found David. God says, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock…" (2 Samuel 7:8). David was out with the sheep, not up in a house.

explanations.answer: A name like the greatest in the land
explanations.explanation: God says, "Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land." (2 Samuel 7:9). He doesn't just remind David of the past. He promises him something new. And you can't carve a name like that on a cookie stamper handle, believe me, I've tried.

explanations.answer: A palace finer than any in the land
explanations.explanation: David already has a palace. The passage opens with him settled into it (2 Samuel 7:1). What God promises is "a name like that of the greatest in the land." (2 Samuel 7:9). That's a name, not another building.

explanations.answer: An army larger than any in the land
explanations.explanation: God does talk about enemies here. He says He has cut them all off from before David. But the next thing He promises is "a name like that of the greatest in the land." (2 Samuel 7:9). No bigger army shows up in this verse.

God says the opposite. He promises, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning…" (2 Samuel 7:10). He also says Israel will "be disturbed no more." That's a big promise for people who've been pushed around.

Right, because God says it's over. "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning…" (2 Samuel 7:10). He says they'll dwell in a place of their own and be disturbed no more. No more getting pushed around.

The LORD says, "…He Himself will establish a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:11). David wanted to build God a house, and God says He'll build David one. And look at who's doing the building, it's "He Himself." David showed up with a cedar idea and got handed a bigger one.

The tent is God's own dwelling in this passage, the one He has moved about with (2 Samuel 7:6). The promise to David is different: "He Himself will establish a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:11). It's a house for David, and God is the one who builds it.
No altar in this promise. God says, "…He Himself will establish a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:11). Here a house means more than walls. He goes on to talk about David's descendant and a kingdom.

God says of David's descendant, "He will build a house for My Name…" (2 Samuel 7:13). So the house David wanted to build gets built after all, just not by David. It's a different builder and the same house idea.

explanations.answer: A wall around the City of David
explanations.explanation: No wall gets mentioned here. God says of David's descendant, "He will build a house for My Name…" (2 Samuel 7:13). That's the building He names.

explanations.answer: A new tent for the ark
explanations.explanation: A tent is what the ark has now, and it's what David was bothered by. But God says David's descendant "will build a house for My Name…" (2 Samuel 7:13). It's a house, not a tent. I've set up plenty of folding tables in my day, but this is something else.

God says, "…I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever." (2 Samuel 7:13). Forever, friend. Not a season, not a term. Some of my cookie boxes don't last till Thursday, so that word hits me hard.
One lifetime is shorter than what God says. He says, "…I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever." (2 Samuel 7:13). The promise runs past any one person's life.
Forty years is a long time, but God says "forever." His words are, "…I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever." (2 Samuel 7:13). There's no number of years attached.

God says, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son." (2 Samuel 7:14). That's a close family word, right in the middle of a promise about a kingdom. David is getting a promise about his own son too.
It's true, though. God says, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son." (2 Samuel 7:14). He says it about David's descendant. That's a Father promising to stand with a son.

God says the opposite. He says, "But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you." (2 Samuel 7:15). Saul was Israel's king before David. David's son gets a different promise than Saul did.

Right. God says, "But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you." (2 Samuel 7:15). Saul was the king before David. God draws the line between the two on purpose, and David's son lands on the better side of it.

explanations.answer: By asking who he is to be brought this far
explanations.explanation: David opens with, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" (2 Samuel 7:18). A king, and the first thing out of his mouth is a question about himself. I think that's a man who knows he didn't get here alone.

explanations.answer: By asking when his son will be born
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask about a birth date. He starts with, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" (2 Samuel 7:18). His first words look back at how far he's come.

explanations.answer: By asking why he can't build the house
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show David arguing about the building. His prayer opens with, "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" (2 Samuel 7:18). He's thinking about the distance he's come, not the project.

David prays, "And as if this was a small thing in Your eyes, O Lord GOD, You have also spoken about the future of the house of Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:19). He's saying God didn't stop at bringing him this far. God also spoke about what's ahead for his house. I think David is still catching his breath.

It's in his prayer. David says, "…as if this was a small thing in Your eyes, O Lord GOD, You have also spoken about the future of the house of Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:19). God gave him the past and the future in one night.

David says, "What more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD." (2 Samuel 7:20). When God already knows you, you don't have to explain yourself. I've stood in front of a customer with my mouth open and no words, so I get it.
Nathan did bring God's words to David (2 Samuel 7:17). But David's reason is, "For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD." (2 Samuel 7:20). His reason is about God knowing him.

explanations.answer: The ark is still in a tent
explanations.explanation: The ark in a tent is what started this whole conversation (2 Samuel 7:2). But David's reason here is, "For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD." (2 Samuel 7:20). He doesn't mention the tent in his prayer at all.

David doesn't say that. He says, "For the sake of Your word and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing…" (2 Samuel 7:21). The reasons he names are God's word and God's own heart, and David's résumé isn't on the list.

Right, he gives God the credit. David prays, "For the sake of Your word and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing…" (2 Samuel 7:21). The credit goes to God's word and God's heart. That's a humble thing for a king to say.
David says the opposite. He prays, "…there is none like You, and there is no God but You…" (2 Samuel 7:22). There's no second LORD on his list.

Right. David says, "…there is none like You, and there is no God but You, according to everything we have heard with our own ears." (2 Samuel 7:22). He says it flat out. None like Him, and no other God.

David says God performed great and awesome wonders "by driving out nations and their gods from before Your people…" (2 Samuel 7:23). So the nations and their gods both went out. David is remembering how God moved ahead of Israel.

David doesn't mention famines or plagues in this prayer. He says the wonders were done "by driving out nations and their gods from before Your people…" (2 Samuel 7:23). The ones driven out are nations and their gods.
No beasts or storms in this line. David says God drove out "nations and their gods from before Your people…" (2 Samuel 7:23). That's who went out before Israel.

David says, "For You have established Your people Israel as Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God." (2 Samuel 7:24). He says it to the LORD directly. Israel belongs to God, and God is their God.
He does say it. David prays that God has established Israel as His own "forever," and adds, "…You, O LORD, have become their God." (2 Samuel 7:24). It's right there in his prayer.

David asks God to do as He promised, "so that Your name will be magnified forever…" (2 Samuel 7:26). The name he wants lifted up is God's own. The king is asking for a big promise, and he points it at God's name.
Nathan brought God's words to David, but his name isn't in this request. David asks "so that Your name will be magnified forever…" (2 Samuel 7:26). The name is God's.
Saul was Israel's king before David, and he doesn't come up in David's prayer. David asks "so that Your name will be magnified forever…" (2 Samuel 7:26). He's talking about God's name.

explanations.answer: God revealed He would build him a house
explanations.explanation: David says God said, "I will build a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:27). Then he adds, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to offer this prayer to You." When God makes the promise first, praying back gets a lot easier. I've walked up to the counter braver after a good sign.

explanations.answer: Nathan told him he should be brave
explanations.explanation: Nathan doesn't tell David to be brave. David points to what God said: "I will build a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:27). He says, "Therefore Your servant has found the courage to offer this prayer to You."

explanations.answer: The people begged him to go pray
explanations.explanation: The people don't show up in this part of the story at all. David's reason is what God said: "I will build a house for you." (2 Samuel 7:27). That's what gave him the courage to pray.

David says, "And now, O Lord GOD, You are God! Your words are true, and You have promised this goodness to Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:28). Then he moves to his last request. He builds on what God said, and he says it's true.
David doesn't say that. He says, "Your words are true, and You have promised this goodness to Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:28). He's confident, not confused.
No sealing in this prayer. David says, "Your words are true, and You have promised this goodness to Your servant." (2 Samuel 7:28). He's talking about promises he's counting on.

David asks, "Now therefore, may it please You to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You." (2 Samuel 7:29). Bless is his ask. He's asking God to do what God already promised.
David doesn't ask God to test his house. He asks, "…may it please You to bless the house of Your servant…" (2 Samuel 7:29). It's a blessing he's after.
David doesn't ask for his house to be humbled. His last request is, "…may it please You to bless the house of Your servant…" (2 Samuel 7:29). He wants blessing, and he asks for it kindly.
